definitions.definition: Five real and eternal differences — God and soul, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, matter and matter — holding in every state including liberation; knowing them is a condition of liberation.
Reality is twofold: the independent, Viṣṇu alone, and the dependent — everything else — which exists, knows and acts only under his control; knowing this frees one from saṃsāra.

Dependent reality divides into negation (prior, posterior, constant) and positive being; positive into sentient (Lakṣmī untouched by sorrow; souls touched by sorrow) and insentient (eternal: Vedas; eternal-and-non-eternal: Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti; non-eternal: uncompounded — mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi, manas, ten senses, five subtle elements, five elements — and compounded — the cosmic egg and its contents).

name: Difference as the nature of things (bheda = svarūpa)

definitions.definition: Difference is not a separate property or negation but the very nature of each thing, apprehended together with the thing itself; hence the Advaita charge of mutual dependence in grasping difference fails.

relations.note: each of the five differences is the nature of its relata

definitions.definition: A thing has no real difference from its lasting properties (and God none from his qualities, acts and forms), yet they can be spoken of distinctly by virtue of viśeṣa; with temporary properties there is difference-and-identity. (Distinct from the Vaiśeṣika category viśeṣa.)

relations.note: viśeṣa accounts for distinctions where there is no real difference

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu is supreme over all — full of qualities, free of defects, beyond the perishable and the imperishable; this is the great purport of all scripture, and 'Brahman' and all names primarily denote him.
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), of the ṛju class and equal in rank with Brahmā, is the highest of souls; no soul equals him; by Viṣṇu's permission he gives liberation, and grace reaches lower beings through him.

name: Vāyu's three avatāras: Hanumān, Bhīma, Madhva

definitions.definition: The tradition holds, on Madhva's own statements reading Ṛgveda 1.141, that Vāyu descended as Hanumān, as Bhīma and, in Kali 4300, as Madhva, to proclaim the truth about Hari; the hagiographies' feats are told as signs of this.

name: Lakṣmī as eternally free and dependent

definitions.definition: Lakṣmī is the highest dependent being: eternally untouched by sorrow, never bound, 'imperishable' (akṣara) in body, superior to all souls in every quality, yet infinitely below and wholly dependent on Viṣṇu; as Śrī, Bhū and Durgā she is the higher prakṛti.

name: Perishable, imperishable and the Supreme Person

definitions.definition: Following Gītā 15.16–18: the perishable are all souls whose bodies perish (Brahmā, Śiva and the gods included); the imperishable is Lakṣmī; the Supreme Person beyond both is Hari.

Brahman is defined as the source of the world's creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release; Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light. God is the efficient cause and controller, not the material cause.

Before creation Nārāyaṇa alone exists, holding all souls in himself with their awareness quiescent, with Lakṣmī; he creates, as his sport, so that embodied souls may reach happiness, sorrow or the mean according to their natures; creation is the real transformation of prakṛti under his control (not of Brahman itself), unfolding into the uncompounded principles and the cosmic egg.

Dvaita: an eternal-and-non-eternal insentient reality, the material cause of the world, dependent on and moved by Viṣṇu, presided over by Lakṣmī; its products are the principles from mahat to the elements. God is not the material cause.
Dvaita: time is eternal (as a flow) and non-eternal (in its divisions), directly perceived by the witness even in deep sleep; everything seen or remembered is set in it.

Dvaita: each soul is eternal, sentient, atomic, dependent, a reflection of God, different from God, from matter and from every other soul, with an innate and unalterable fitness; its identity with Brahman is denied as contrary to experience and scripture.

name: The soul as God's reflection (bimba–pratibimba, Dvaita sense)

definitions.definition: The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God, its original (bimba): dependent on him, resembling him, and eternally different; the reflecting 'adjunct' is the soul's own nature, so the relation is eternal. The worshipper contemplates: 'You are the original, I am the reflection, though there is a difference between us.' (Not the Advaita reflection theory, in which the reflection is Brahman appearing in an adjunct.)
Each soul's innate, beginningless fitness fixes its class, office, the form of worship and vision open to it and its final destiny; it cannot be altered, and to aim beyond it leads to a fall.

Souls are graded, beginninglessly and endlessly, in knowledge, bliss and office — from humans and kings up through gandharvas, ancestors, gods, Indra, Rudra, to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Lakṣmī above and Viṣṇu infinitely above; the gradation is unalterable and continues in liberation, and knowing it is required for liberation.

By nature souls are of three classes: fit for liberation (gods, sages, ancestors, rulers, the best humans), ever-transmigrating (middling humans), and fit for blinding darkness (daityas, rākṣasas, piśācas, the lowest humans). The texts state this plainly; souls of the third class reach darkness especially through hatred of Hari.

relations.note: the three classes are the broadest division of the gradation

definitions.definition: The eternal state of sorrow, without return, reached by the souls fit for darkness; the texts connect it with hatred of Viṣṇu and his devotees and with the conceit 'I am ever the Lord and the world is unreal'.

Dvaita: the soul's own intrinsic faculty of awareness (its essential sense), the seventh kind of perception; it apprehends the self, mind and its states, pleasure and pain, time and space, and the validity of knowledge; its deliverances are infallible and never sublated, and it is the final guarantor of knowledge, including the reality of the world.

relations.note: the witness establishes the world's reality

name: Knowledge-itself and the means of knowledge (kevala / anupramāṇa)

definitions.definition: Valid knowledge is what accords with its object; it is knowledge itself (of God, Lakṣmī, yogins, others) and its three means (perception, inference, authoritative word); memory is valid; presumption and comparison are inference.
Dvaita: validity is intrinsic and is grasped by the witness; reasoning only removes doubts in a defective intellect; invalidity is extrinsic.

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth as forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: Dvaita reads the Māṇḍūkya's four quarters as four forms of the Supreme Self in all beings: Viśva presiding over waking, Taijasa creating dreams in the mind, Prājña lord of deep sleep, and Turīya at the dvādaśānta, attained by the liberated. The soul experiences the states; God governs them.

relations.note: Prājña is the form presiding over deep sleep

definitions.definition: Dreams are not false: they are produced from latent impressions (vāsanā) by the Lord as Taijasa abiding in the mind.
In deep sleep the soul, covered by tamas, rests in Hari as Prājña, neither desiring nor seeing; yet the witness still perceives time (and the self), so deep sleep is not the absence of all awareness.

name: Mind and its parts in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Mahat, ahaṃkāra, buddhi and manas are non-eternal, uncompounded products of prakṛti; manas is the sixth sense; memory arises from mental perception; above all these stands the witness, the soul's own awareness.

The heart has a hundred and one channels; the one rising to the crown (suṣumnā) is the knower's path at death; in seated worship the suṣumnā is contemplated as shining, lit above the crown by the sun's rays.

name: Ignorance (avidyā)

definitions.definition: Dvaita: a real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold — one hiding the soul's own nature and qualities, one hiding (its knowledge of) the Supreme; only the Lord removes them and grants liberation. It does not affect God or the self-luminous in the Advaita sense; Madhva's refutations deny ignorance of a self-luminous, attributeless Brahman.

members: covering of the soul's own qualities

relations.note: the second covering hides the knowledge of the Supreme

name: The Lord as the real agent (hari-kartṛtva)

definitions.definition: The soul's acts are done by Hari's impulsion within it; one performs prescribed duties without desire, remembering Hari as doer and goal, so that all activity of mind, speech and body is his worship — this is 'yoga'.

Seekers are low, middle or highest by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant with sole refuge in Viṣṇu; eligibility for the Veda, the Tantra and the Name differs by class and gender, and the Mahābhārata was composed for those not entitled to the Veda.
Grace won by ritual works is lowest and yields heaven; won by hearing and the like is middling and yields higher worlds; won by fullness of knowledge is highest and alone yields liberation.

relations.note: grace is graded by its means

definitions.definition: Dvaita: hearing, reflection, meditation and devotion are the principal means to knowledge; meditation, not a mere subsidiary of hearing, produces the direct realization by which the Lord is pleased; hearing and the rest must never be reduced.

relations.note: meditation built on hearing produces direct realization

definitions.definition: Direct realization of God, which wins his highest grace; the gods are liberated when Hari becomes directly perceived to them; its scope is limited by fitness — few may see him as all-pervading, most see him within their own body.

relations.note: without knowledge there is no abundant grace

name: Vision limited by fitness — the warning against striving for an unfit vision

definitions.definition: One may see God only in the manner one's fitness allows; one who strives for a vision (or office) he is unfit for falls even from what he had; so service is to be rendered according to fitness.

relations.note: the limits of vision follow from intrinsic fitness

definitions.definition: Dvaita: liberation comes only by Viṣṇu's grace (his 'choosing'); knowledge and devotion win it; it is graded, and it reaches lower beings through the higher (Vāyu and the gods).

relations.note: without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation

name: Grace through the hierarchy of souls

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu gives liberation, Vāyu by his permission; liberation, knowledge and their fruits come to the lower by the grace of the higher, not otherwise.

Dvaita: firm love for Viṣṇu, greater than love for anything else, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation to which gifts, pilgrimage, austerity and sacrifice are subsidiary; it continues in liberation as eternal bliss.

relations.note: by bhakti is liberation, not otherwise

definitions.definition: Karma cannot be exhausted by experiencing it, for new karma is always made; ritual works win only the lowest grace (heaven); release needs grace won by knowledge; prārabdha karma still runs its course.

Release from saṃsāra by Viṣṇu's grace into the unobstructed enjoyment of one's own bliss, in eternal difference from and dependence on him, in forms such as sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya and sāyujya, graded by fitness, with bhakti continuing and the liberated desiring only in accord with the Lord's will; not the mere cessation of ignorance.
The liberated soul remains different from Brahman and from other souls; the five differences and gradation 'are not lost even for the liberated'.

relations.note: the five differences hold 'even for the liberated'

definitions.definition: Even in liberation bliss is graded: each class of the liberated enjoys a hundredfold more than the one below, up to Brahmā and Vāyu, with Śrī far above and Viṣṇu infinitely above.

relations.note: gradation continues in liberation as graded bliss

name: Liberation together with Brahmā at the dissolution

definitions.definition: Knowers who go by the path of light to Brahmā's world reach the Supreme together with Brahmā at the great dissolution; some others are liberated without departing.
At death the tip of the heart lights up and the knower leaves through the crown channel by the power of knowledge and remembrance, helped by the grace of Hari in the heart.

name: Teacher, lineage and initiation in Dvaita

definitions.definition: Knowledge descends from Nārāyaṇa (as Vyāsa, author of the Brahmasūtras) through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge from the teacher's grace, hears the commentaries and reflects on them with companions; the ācārya initiates the prepared devotee into Hari's worship; renunciants receive the praṇava and new names; debate (vāda) between teacher and disciple serves the truth.

Viṣṇu is known only through the true scriptures — the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa, consonant Purāṇas and works that follow them — not by reasoning alone or the senses; other texts are false scriptures, some produced to delude.
Dvaita: the Veda has no author, not even God; it is eternal and intrinsically valid.
Every word, in its primary sense, names Viṣṇu — 'Brahman', 'Agni', 'Indra' and the rest — and only secondarily other beings; ritual texts too have him as purport.

name: The eightfold praṇava

definitions.definition: Om is the designator of Viṣṇu and has eight components, from 'a' to 'atiśānta', naming eight of his forms (Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, Turīya, Ātman, Antarātman, Paramātman, Jñānātman); the other mantras derive from it.

members: nāda, bindu, ghoṣa, śānta (intermediate names recalled, not verified)

name: Fifty letters, fifty forms of Viṣṇu

definitions.definition: The fifty letters designate fifty forms of Viṣṇu — Aja, Ānanda, Indra, Īśa, Ugra, Ūrja, Ṛtambhara and so on — used in nyāsa and worship.

name: The threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata

definitions.definition: The Bhārata has three levels of meaning: the narrative of the Pāṇḍavas with Kṛṣṇa (āstīka), the teaching of dharma, devotion and conduct (manvādi), and the reading of all its words as names of Nārāyaṇa (auparicara).

name: The marks of purport (liṅga) in Dvaita exegesis

definitions.definition: Opening and conclusion, their agreement, repetition, novelty, result and praise — with reasoning — are the marks of a text's purport; name, sentence, context and position are further marks.

Dvaita: the avatāras are Viṣṇu himself manifesting his eternal body of consciousness and bliss, flawless and without internal difference; apparent human weakness is displayed to delude the unfit. One must also know which beings are merely indwelt (āveśa).

The world is real, established by perception, scripture ('viśvaṃ satyam') and above all the witness, whose deliverances are never sublated; the Advaita definitions of falsity and inferences to it fail.

Dvaita's case against Advaita: ignorance cannot belong to a self-luminous attributeless self or to the all-knower; the indeterminable is unproven; the world's falsity is unproven; 'māyā' in scripture means God's will; and an attributeless Brahman is indistinguishable from the Mādhyamika void.

name: 'Atat tvam asi' — Dvaita's reading of Chāndogya 6.8.7

definitions.definition: The Chāndogya teaching repeated nine times with examples is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), or 'aitadātmya' as being under the Lord's control; it teaches difference, and the conceit of identity is condemned.

relations.note: the reading of 6.8.7 is one plank of the critique of Advaita
